verdicts.critic: Neutrality: PASS. This is at or above parity with a strong published topic on my dimension. Nine camps span the real spectrum (deregulate, horizontal law, model-level mandates, sectoral, international, pause, open-weights, present-harms/power, national-security), each gets a banner-grade steelman in its own voice, and every position detail follows the same three-part structure — the camp's own best evidence, its internal split, and an explicit answer to the sharpest objection against it. That structural symmetry is what keeps the deregulatory camps (Innovation-First, Sectoral, Open-Weights) from being set up to be knocked down, which is the failure mode this topic invites. Prevalence weights run 80 down to 15 rather than flattening to 50/50, so asymmetry is carried honestly. The crux presupposes a location for the rule, not an answer, and the values axis is left genuinely open. No house verdict anywhere. Directional check: four question `why` lines lean, but in three different directions (against industry's competitiveness claim, against regulators' threshold tools, against voluntary pledges, toward present harms), so nothing accumulates into a site position, and each detail restores the balance. CAVEAT ON MY COVERAGE CHECK: the session's web search budget was fully exhausted before I could run any searches, so the missing-camp check below is from knowledge, not fresh search. If a human editor wants a hard guarantee on 2026 developments, that check should be re-run with search available. On what I can assess, the two candidate gaps (a liability/insurance-first camp, and the child-safety/consumer-protection coalition) are both mechanism- or scope-boundary questions rather than orphaned constituencies, and both are partially carried by existing camps — notes, not blockers.
notes: Strongest coverage candidate: a liability-first camp has no home. scope_covered explicitly names 'liability', but no position owns it and no question asks it — liability appears only as a passing mechanism inside Frontier Safety Mandater ('testing and liability duties') and Present-Harms ('enforcement, liability and disclosure duties'). There is a real, currently-active school arguing for expanded strict liability and insurance markets INSTEAD of ex-ante rules (Gabriel Weil, Institute for Law & AI, Ketan Ramakrishnan at RAND, insurance-market proposals). Judgment call for the editor: it is a cross-cutting mechanism rather than a constituency, so folding it is defensible — but if it stays folded, consider dropping 'liability' from scope_covered or adding a question on ex-ante rules versus ex-post liability, since the scope line currently promises something the body does not deliver.

Second coverage candidate, a scope-boundary call: the child-safety / consumer-protection coalition (state AGs, Common Sense Media, the GUARD Act, California SB 243, parents' groups) is arguably the single most decisive political actor in the US preemption fight, and the draft itself credits it — the Innovation-First detail says the moratorium died because 'even sympathetic Republicans balked at preempting state child-safety and consumer-protection laws.' It appears only as a footnote inside another camp's detail. scope_excluded covers 'application-level AI fights', which plausibly reaches it, so this is probably correctly out of scope — but the draft leans on this constituency to explain the 99-1 vote while giving it no voice, which a reader may notice.

Basics carries no shared anchor for the competitiveness dimension. The two most prominent risk-salient facts (the 5-10% extinction survey, first stat on the page; the 3 lab CEOs signing the extinction statement) are elevated into shared Basics, while the empirical core of the highest-prevalence camp (weight 80) — $109.1B vs $9.3B private investment, 38 states enacting ~100 measures — lives only inside that camp's own description. Net valence across the ten stats is roughly balanced (the incident-DB 'none of them mass-casualty' line and the Council of Europe 'binds nobody' line both cut deflationary), so this does not mislead, but a shared stat on the state-patchwork count or on US/China investment would let a reader weigh Q2 and Q3 from the shared layer rather than from one camp's advocacy.

Actions rail has a small visible asymmetry: Frontier Safety Mandater is the only camp with two actions (Encode tier 1 plus a CAIS donate at tier 2), and Sectoral Incrementalist is the only camp relegated to tier 2. Cheap fix: promote the R Street action to tier 1, or drop the CAIS donate, so every camp gets exactly one tier-1 entry.

Innovation-First's action points to American Edge Project, which is widely reported as industry-funded advocacy, while every other camp gets its actual intellectual home (R Street, AI Now, Mozilla's letter, nationalsecurity.ai, the Commission's own AI Act page). Consider a16z's Little Tech Agenda or the Abundance Institute for a more representative and less contestable choice.

Pause Advocate's third detail paragraph opens in narrator voice on a contested empirical claim: 'Even the labs building frontier models cannot fully explain why a given model produces a given output: interpretability lags capability by a wide and growing margin.' Every other camp's comparable claims are attributed. 'Growing margin' is genuinely contested given recent mechanistic-interpretability work. Attribute it ('Pause advocates point out that...') to match the surrounding convention.

Q5's `why` states only the critics' case ('compute thresholds ... get cheaper to cross every year', 'benchmark-based triggers age even faster') with no framing for the supporters, even though the detail balances it properly. Low prominence (tier 3, deep), but a half-clause fix restores parity: note that supporters answer an imperfect auditable line still beats none and is revisable by rulemaking.

Q6's `why` asserts one side's characterization as established fact ('have made, and in several documented cases quietly loosened') before offering both readings. Defensible and self-correcting, but this is a tier-1 condensed question, the highest-prominence layer, and it pairs with the most lopsided lean in the set (20/80). Consider a more neutral verb ('revised', 'relaxed') and letting the two readings carry the charge.

spectrum_position places National Security Realist at +2, the same slot as Open-Weights Advocate, despite NSR wanting export licensing over model weights themselves — close to the opposite of the open-weights ask. Defensible if the axis is light-touch-on-civilian-products, but it reads oddly against the crux's stated 'how far upstream binding rules reach' axis, on which NSR sits well toward the restrictive end.

Outside my dimension but worth one sweep before publish: straight apostrophes appear in roughly two dozen places ("Biden's", "OpenAI's", "South Korea's", "NTIA's", "DeepSeek's", "AI Now's", "camp's") mixed with curly ones elsewhere; 'U.S.' in why_now versus 'US' throughout the body; and '10^25 FLOP' / '10^25 FLOPs' / '10^25 floating-point operations' all appear. Also five of the ten Basics stats cite Wikipedia where a primary source exists (leginfo for SB 53, the Bletchley Declaration text, the CAIS statement page).

verdicts.critic:
Steelman review of the frontier-AI-regulation draft. Verdict: pass — no blocking defects on my dimension.

Nine positions, all tier 1, and every one is written in its own voice with a banner-ready one-liner a real proponent would sign. I checked each for the usual tells of a softened side (a critic's framing smuggled into the card, a concession paragraph with no recovery, an evidentiary thinness relative to its rivals) and found none that mislead.

Coverage: the map is unusually complete — innovation-first, horizontal/EU, frontier-safety mandates, sectoral, global coordination, pause, open-weights, present-harms accountability, national-security. The camps most often strawmanned in this debate get the fairest treatment here: Present-Harms Accountability lands its agenda-setting critique ("the catastrophic-risk frame is not neutral either") without being reduced to "they just don't believe in x-risk", Pause Advocate preempts the unilateral-pause objection rather than being left holding it, and Sectoral Incrementalist answers the GPAI-cuts-across-sectors objection head on instead of ducking it. Innovation-First gets real evidence (the 2025 patchwork, the $109.1B/$9.3B investment gap, 40 vs 15 notable models) rather than a caricature, and its own AI Index citation is turned into its warning shot — that is in-voice, not a house rebuttal.

Symmetry of concessions: every position's detail carries an internal-split or hard-objection paragraph, so no camp is uniquely made to eat its weaknesses. Basics are genuinely two-directional — the incident-database entry ("none of them mass-casualty or civilization-scale") and the CoE treaty entry ("binds nobody until five countries ratify") cut against the safety and coordination camps, while the researcher-survey and compute-growth entries cut the other way. The extinction-risk stat carries its own counterweights (68% net optimism, "many researchers reject the exercise as unfalsifiable").

No house verdict. The crux poses the burden-of-proof question symmetrically and does not resolve it. I confirmed in topics/models.py and templates/topics/components/_qlean.html that lean_pct_a is a research seed only — percentages and the bar stay hidden until reader votes reach MIN_STANCE_SAMPLE — so the several strongly tilted editorial leans (20/80 on voluntary commitments, 30/70 on near-term risk) never surface to a reader as an editorial call.

Facts and links: all source URLs resolve (coe.int, encodeai.org and americanedgeproject.org 403 to curl but are live WAF-protected pages; I fetched the latter two and both match their descriptions). Spot-verified SB 53's signing date of September 25 2025, the 10^26 FLOP and $500M thresholds, the 15-day reporting duty and the 50-deaths/$1B catastrophic definition, EO 14365, EO 14148's revocation of EO 14110, the 99-1 Senate vote, and the RAISE Act's December 19 2025 signing and January 1 2027 effective date. The NCSL patchwork figures, AI Index investment and model counts, EU fine tiers, RAND's 38 attack vectors, the NIST 10-to-100x false-match finding, and the NTIA report's 332 comments all check out against what I know. Nothing wrong or misattributed surfaced.

The closest thing to a gap is that the labs' own operating position — RSPs and frontier safety frameworks as the governing regime — has no card of its own and lives only as one half of Q6 plus a paragraph inside Frontier Safety Mandater. That is defensible given Innovation-First and Sectoral already cover the anti-mandate ground, and it does not rise to a missing major position, but it is where the draft is thinnest and where the one real asymmetry sits (see notes).
notes: Q6 (voluntary commitments) is the one genuinely asymmetric pairing. The pro-voluntary half gestures at evidence without naming any ("instances where labs have delayed releases, published model cards, or withheld capabilities"), while the critic half is specific ("testing windows compressed as competitive launches clustered", "several signatories shipped capabilities the pledges were meant to gate"). Name one concrete instance on the pro side — a release delayed or heightened safeguards activated under a lab's own published framework — so both halves carry the same evidentiary weight.

Q6's 'why' line asserts the erosion camp's factual claim as shared framing ("have made, and in several documented cases quietly loosened, voluntary safety pledges") and only then offers the alternative reading as an interpretation. Recasting it so both readings sit at the same level ("labs have loosened published commitments as release schedules tightened, which reads either as ... or as ...") would keep the framing layer neutral. The current wording is close to that already; it is the ordering that tilts.

The labs' own self-governance position (responsible scaling policies / frontier safety frameworks as the regime, not a stopgap) is the only recognizable camp without a card. It is adequately covered between Innovation-First, Sectoral, and the Frontier Safety Mandater detail, so this is not a gap that misleads — but if a tenth card is ever added, that is the one.

Frontier Safety Mandater is the only position with two actions (Encode plus the CAIS donate). Innovation-First carries the highest prevalence weight at 80 and has one. Not misleading, but the action shelf currently over-serves the smaller camp.

American Edge Project is a defensible representative for Innovation-First — its site copy tracks the card's argument almost line for line — but it is an industry-backed coalition, whereas the other camps get institutions that are straightforwardly what they claim (Encode, AI Now, Mozilla, R Street). a16z's Little Tech Agenda or the America's AI Action Plan page would be a stronger, less-contestable destination for that camp.

Innovation-First's middle paragraph is the only internal-split section organized around a legislative defeat rather than a disagreement over means. It recovers well ("That defeat didn't kill the goal, it redirected it"), but leading with the redirect and treating the 99-1 loss as the reason for it would read more like the camp's own account of itself.

The crux subtitle sets the axis floor at "liability after the fact". Innovation-First and Sectoral both argue for no new frontier-specific binding rules at all, which sits a notch below that floor. "From existing law enforced after the fact to a halt on scaling" would seat both camps inside the axis.

Apostrophe register is mixed and needs one sweep before publish. Curly throughout Innovation-First, Comprehensive Regulator, Frontier Safety Mandater and Pause; straight ASCII in Open-Weights, Present-Harms Accountability, parts of National Security Realist, and several basics notes and details ("OpenAI's Sam Altman", "Biden's 2023 AI executive order", "NTIA's report", "DeepSeek's R1", "AI Now's", "the camp's", "World's first", "a higher-compute one's performance").

Post-cutoff specifics that are load-bearing in their sections and worth one final verification pass before publish: the June 2026 Commerce extension of licensing to certain frontier Anthropic models and EO 14409 (National Security Realist, cited twice), the Digital Omnibus in force July 27 2026 (basics and Comprehensive Regulator), the FDA list at 1,524 authorizations published June 2026 (Sectoral, its headline number), and the 70,000+ signature count on the Statement on Superintelligence (Pause). None appear wrong; all sit past what I could independently confirm.

Minor unit style in basics: "3.5x a year" and "10,000-fold" mix an ASCII x with the multiplication sign used elsewhere ("5 ×/year"). Also worth sanity-checking the internal arithmetic there — 5x/year compounded since 2020 implies more than 10,000-fold, so the two figures in that entry may be describing slightly different series.

verdicts.critic:
Fact-source pass on "frontier-ai-regulation". Web search budget was exhausted at the start of this session, so I verified by direct fetch of every source and action URL in the draft plus primary documents. Nothing I could check came back wrong, and no link is dead. Verdict: pass.

VERIFIED EXACTLY AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCES

Grace et al. (arxiv.org/abs/2401.02843, live): 2,778 published AI researchers confirmed from the abstract. I pulled the HTML full text to check the medians and means the detail asserts: Q1 median 5% / mean 16.2% (n=1,321), Q2 "human inability to control future advanced AI systems" median 10% / mean 19.4% (n=661), Q3 median 5% / mean 14.4% (n=655). The draft's "median 5 percent, rising to 10 percent when the question was phrased as human inability to control advanced AI; means ran far higher, 14 to 19 percent" is exactly right, including the means range. "Between 38 and 51 percent" and "68 percent thought good outcomes more likely than bad" both match the abstract (68.3%). This is the one stat where a sloppy draft usually breaks, and it holds.

Epoch AI (epoch.ai/trends, live): every number matches the page. 5x/year training compute growth (doubling 5.2 months), ~10,000x since 2020, cost 3.5x/year "doubling every 7 months" (the page uses the same phrasing), algorithmic efficiency divided by 3.0x/year — which is precisely the draft's "cut the compute needed for equivalent performance by roughly two-thirds a year."

EU AI Act (Commission page, live): entry into force 1 Aug 2024, prohibitions 2 Feb 2025, GPAI 2 Aug 2025, general application 2 Aug 2026, and the Digital Omnibus deferral to 2 Dec 2027 (stand-alone high-risk) and 2 Aug 2028 (product-embedded) all confirmed on the Commission's own page. The 10^25 FLOP systemic-risk threshold confirmed verbatim at artificialintelligenceact.eu.

California SB 53: 10^26 FLOP, $500M revenue floor, 15-day reporting (immediate if imminent), 50+ deaths/serious injuries or $1B in economic damage, signed 25 Sept 2025 — all confirmed.

US preemption fight: Senate 99-1 on 2 July 2025; EO 14110 (30 Oct 2023) revoked by EO 14148 (Jan 2025); EO 14365 "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for AI," signed 11 Dec 2025, working through funding conditions and DOJ litigation with a child-safety carve-out. The why_now framing is accurate.

Also confirmed: Bletchley 28 countries, 1 Nov 2023, and the full summit series through New Delhi 2026 and Geneva 2027; Mozilla Joint Statement at exactly 1,821 signatories with LeCun and Ng named; AI Now "Artificial Power" by Brennan/Kak/Myers West, 3 June 2025; Superintelligence Strategy authorship and its three pillars (MAIM, nonproliferation, competitiveness); RAISE Act signed 19 Dec 2025, effective 1 Jan 2027.

LINK CHECK: all 11 action URLs and all source URLs resolve and match their descriptions (PauseAI, Encode, FLI, CAIS donate, American Edge, R Street commentary — live, dated March 2026, Thierer and Kolas, and it does argue existing sectoral law reaches AI harms). The one exception is coe.int, which returns 403. I tested a second, unrelated coe.int URL and it also 403s, so this is site-wide bot-blocking, not a dead link — it will work for a human reader but will trip an automated link checker.

DURABILITY: strong, and better than most drafts I see. Eight of ten Basics stats are structural (compute-growth trend, statutory thresholds, treaty ratification conditions) or fixed historical facts (99-1, 28 countries, 3 CEOs). The only running counter is the AI Incident Database tally, and it is handled correctly: framed as a floor ("1,600+"), explicitly described as a crowdsourced running tally with its sampling bias named, and dated. I confirmed the count — the live site is serving incidents 1627 through 1632, so the floor holds. The genuinely perishable items in the Council of Europe detail ("roughly 20 signatories... by mid-2026," "no entry-into-force date had been announced as of August 2026") are both explicitly dated, which is the right treatment.

WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY (notes, not blockers — no evidence any is wrong): the FDA device counts, the June 2026 Commerce model-licensing action, and the RAISE Act penalty figures. FDA's AI-enabled device list 404s from all three URL paths I tried, so the page has moved; I could not confirm 1,524 or the 346 baseline. These sit in position detail text, which carries no source field by schema, so they are not unsourced links — but they are the load-bearing evidence for their positions and deserve a human check before publish.

No house verdict, no false balance, and no strawman detected in the fact layer. Prevalence weights (80 down to 15, Pause lowest) track real-world distribution sensibly.
notes: Sourcing hierarchy: five of ten Basics stats cite Wikipedia (SB 53 twice, US AI regulation, AI Safety Summit, Statement on AI Risk). Every fact checks out and every link is live, so this is not a defect — but the house rule prefers primary/official, and the primaries here are easy swaps: California's legislative text for SB 53 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), the Federal Register for EO 14365, and the CAIS statement page (safe.ai/statement-on-ai-risk) for the extinction statement.

Verify before publish — FDA counts: the Sectoral Incrementalist description leans on '1,524 authorizations, up from 346 cumulative through the end of 2020,' attributed to a list FDA published June 2026 covering decisions through March 2026. FDA's AI-enabled device list 404s from all three URL paths I tried, so the page has moved and I could not confirm either number. This is the position's single strongest piece of evidence; confirm the current total and the 2020 baseline, and note that a device count is a running figure that will need a bump each time it is updated.

Verify before publish — export-control chain: the National Security Realist detail asserts a 15% H20 revenue share (Aug 2025), 25% extended to the H200 (Dec 2025), a 25% semiconductor tariff proclamation (Jan 2026), and — most strikingly — that in June 2026 Commerce extended export licensing beyond hardware for the first time to require a license for certain frontier Anthropic models, plus EO 14409. I could not confirm any of the post-2025 items from reachable sources. The Anthropic model-licensing claim is unusually specific and is the camp's 'actual track record' anchor, so it should be confirmed against a BIS or Federal Register citation.

Verify before publish — RAISE Act penalties: signing date (19 Dec 2025) and effective date (1 Jan 2027) are confirmed, but the $1M first-violation / $3M subsequent caps and the 72-hour reporting duty are not. The bill as passed carried substantially higher penalties, and the draft attributes the reduction to a 27 March 2026 chapter amendment. The trajectory is internally consistent across two places in the draft, but confirm the final figures — a dropped zero here would be a real error.

Precision: the 10^26-vs-10^25 stat detail says algorithmic efficiency means 'a lower-compute model can match a higher-compute one's performance within roughly a year.' At Epoch's confirmed rate of divide-by-3.0x/year, one year buys a 3x compute reduction; closing the specific 10x EU/California gap the stat just displayed takes closer to two years. The sentence is generic enough not to be false, but placed right after a 10x comparison it invites the wrong reading. Consider 'within about two years' or naming the 3x-per-year rate directly.

The EEOC reference in the Sectoral Incrementalist detail — 'The EEOC's 2023 guidance applying existing Title VII and ADA analysis to algorithmic hiring tools' — merges two separate documents issued in different years: the ADA guidance (May 2022) and the Title VII guidance (May 2023). Split them or drop the year.

Encode's representative_note says it 'sponsored both SB 53 and the RAISE Act.' Encode's own site claims sponsorship of SB 53 but describes its RAISE Act role as having 'helped pass' it. Soften the second verb to match the source.

The Pause Advocate detail cites 'over 70,000 signatures' on the Statement on Superintelligence. As a floor claim it is not wrong, but that statement's count climbed steeply after launch and the figure may now understate it considerably. Recheck and attach a date, since this is a running counter inside otherwise durable text.

Comprehensive Regulator phrases the GPAI penalty as 'fines up to 3 percent of global turnover, or 15 million euros.' The Act sets these as whichever is higher, not an either/or — a reader could take the euro figure as a cap on the percentage. Add 'whichever is higher.'

The NIST face-recognition figure in Present-Harms Accountability ('false matches for Asian and Black faces 10 to 100 times more often than white ones across many algorithms') is accurate but undated, and it is specific to false positives in one-to-one verification. Given the house rule on isolating and dating figures, add the year (2019, NISTIR 8280) and ideally the matching mode.

The Council of Europe source URL returns 403 to automated fetches. I confirmed this is coe.int bot-blocking rather than a dead link — a second coe.int URL 403s identically — so it works for readers, but flag it so a future automated link-check run does not report it as broken.

Voluntary-vs-binding (question 6, tier 1 / condensed) is the one live axis the crux does not clearly carry. "How far upstream of demonstrated harm binding rules should reach" presumes the rule is binding; the Innovation-First and Open-Weights answer "self-governance plus monitoring, no new binding rule" sits slightly off-axis. Could be absorbed by widening the first axis's downstream anchor, e.g. "from a voluntary commitment or liability after the fact, to a halt on scaling."

The lead's third rung, "the training run itself," is doing double duty: it houses Pause Advocate (stop the run) and National Security Realist (govern the compute and the weights that feed it). Those are different bites at the same stage. If a sharper triad is wanted, "at the use, the model, or the compute behind it?" locates NSR more explicitly while still holding Pause; the current wording works but leans Pause-ward.

Mild redundancy between the subtitle's second axis ("at what level the rule gets written, a statehouse, a capital, or a treaty") and the closing clause of the values field ("who legitimately holds the pen ... states, nations, or international bodies"). The values field could spend that space on the openness dimension instead, since transparency-as-safety-mechanism is Open-Weights' actual first premise and appears nowhere in the crux.

The empirical field's final clause elides a second "whether" across a comma: "whether binding rules measurably slow capability progress, and any slowdown actually cedes a decisive geopolitical lead." Reads slightly clipped; "and whether any slowdown" would settle it.

"Where should the law bite" presupposes the law bites somewhere, which is a fair framing given no camp in the field argues for literally zero rules (Innovation-First wants one light federal standard, Open-Weights wants monitoring plus capability-specific limits). Worth keeping in mind only if a genuine no-rules camp is ever added.

verdicts.critic: Read at the fold only, this draft holds up well. The six above-fold basics span the evidence base (researcher risk estimates, incident record), the capability trend (compute growth), and all three live regulatory arenas (EU Act phase-in, the US preemption fight, California SB 53) — a reader who stops there gets a correct map of what is being regulated, by whom, and why the timing is contested. All four above-fold question whys do real work rather than restating their question, and the six visible steelmen are each intelligible standing alone. The crux lead plus subtitle name both axes (how far upstream, and who writes the rule) without needing the empirical/values expansions. No compact line contradicts or is reversed by its detail, and no above-fold value is stranded without the caveat that makes it readable — the incident-database note carries "crowdsourced" and "none of them mass-casualty" in the note itself, which is exactly where they belong. Remaining issues are trims and one label/unit scope mismatch, all note-level: nothing above the fold sends a reader away with a wrong picture.
notes: Label/value scope mismatch, stat 4 (AI Incident Database): the label says 'Documented real-world AI harm reports' but the value counts incidents ('1,600+ / incidents logged'), and in that database reports vastly outnumber incidents. The unit corrects it, but the label should match: change label to 'Documented real-world AI harm incidents · AI Incident Database'.

Stat 6 (SB 53, $1 billion): who actually owes the 15-day report is detail-only ('large frontier developers': revenue above $500 million, models above 10^26 FLOP). Above the fold the duty reads as universal to AI companies. Cheap fix inside the note, no new fact: 'Fifty or more deaths or serious injuries counts as catastrophic too, and crossing either line means large frontier developers must report to the state within 15 days, or immediately if harm is imminent.'

Stat 1 (researcher risk estimates) tilts one way at the fold: the note pairs the 5-10 percent median with '38 to 51 percent... 10 percent or more', while the counterweight already in the detail (68 percent of the same respondents thought good outcomes from superhuman AI more likely than bad) never surfaces. Consider replacing or following the 38-51 clause with that counterweight so the compact layer reads as the survey does.

Stat 2 note refers to 'a fixed threshold' drifting from frontier toward ordinary, but nothing above the fold has established that laws use compute thresholds at all — the EU vs California threshold stat is T2, below the fold. One naming clause in the note (e.g. 'so a compute threshold written into law drifts...') makes the sentence self-standing.

'Weights' appears unexplained in two of the six above-fold steelmen (Open-Weights Advocate: 'a model you aren't allowed to have'; National Security Realist: 'govern the chips and the weights'). Compact register bars unexplained terms of art. The Open-Weights steelman survives on its own phrasing; consider making the National Security Realist one concrete, e.g. 'govern the chips and the trained models themselves'.

Structural, not a defect to fix here: prevalence ordering puts Present-Harms Accountability seventh (below fold) and the present-vs-catastrophic question at T2, so the above-fold layer frames the debate mainly as catastrophic risk vs speed. The AI Incident Database stat above the fold partly offsets this by putting documented present-day harm in view, which is why it does not read as a tilt.
Register slip visible in compact copy: why_now writes 'U.S. executive order' while every other compact label and note uses 'US' ('US preemption fight', 'the US, China, the EU and UK'). Make it 'US'.

verdicts.critic: Reading-level fit is strong overall: the compact layer mostly reads at the smart-general-reader bar (the EU AI Act phase-in, the 99–1 Senate vote, the incident-database tally, and every position steelman land cleanly), and the expanded layer genuinely adds — question 'detail' fields are exemplary two-sided expansions with mechanism the 'why' line never carries, and the stat details reliably supply provenance, methodology caveats, and precise figures the notes deliberately round away. One defect blocks: the compute-threshold stat carries a bare, never-expanded acronym in its own label and unit, so the reader's takeaway number ("10^26 FLOP") means nothing at the compact layer. Everything else is trim-level.

blocking.issue: Basics stat 'Training-compute threshold, in FLOP, that triggers binding duties · EU vs California' (tier 2): FLOP is a bare acronym in three compact fields at once — label ('in FLOP'), unit (' FLOP'), and the headline value ('10^26'). Nothing in the compact layer anywhere on the page expands it; the only spelled-out instance ('floating-point operations') is buried in the Comprehensive Regulator description. A general reader sees '10^26 FLOP' as the stat's retainable number and gets nothing from it.
blocking.fix: Gloss the term once in the compact layer of this stat. Label → 'Training-compute threshold that triggers binding duties · EU vs California' (drop 'in FLOP'); open the note with the expansion: 'Both regimes count floating-point operations (FLOP), the raw arithmetic a training run burns: California set its bar a full order of magnitude above the EU’s, and both use training compute as a proxy for capability rather than capability itself.' Unit may stay 'FLOP' once the note defines it. No fact, number, or source changes.

notes: Same stat, series label 'EU AI Act (systemic-risk GPAI)': GPAI is a second bare acronym, never expanded anywhere in the compact layer. Suggest 'EU AI Act (general-purpose models with systemic risk)'.

Comprehensive Regulator representative_note: 'GPAI duties binding from August 2025' repeats the unexpanded acronym on a short card line, and 'horizontal AI law' is a term of art there too. Suggest 'general-purpose model duties binding from August 2025' and letting 'tiering obligations by risk' (already in the linked action description) carry the 'horizontal' idea.

Question 1 why: 'rising scores on bioweapon uplift and autonomous cyber-offense' — 'uplift' is insider vocabulary for how much a model boosts a novice's capability, and this is a T1 above-fold compact line. The detail defines the idea ('synthesizing dangerous biological information'); consider pulling that plainer phrasing up, e.g. 'rising scores on how much a model helps a novice with bioweapon design and on running cyberattacks unaided'.

National Security Realist steelman: 'govern the chips and the weights' leaves 'weights' unglossed in a compact punchline. The position's own description resolves it one layer down ('the model weights themselves'), so it survives, but 'govern the chips and the model files' would cost nothing.

Mild detail-restates-compact overlap, all still net-additive so none blocking: the AI Incident Database detail closes by repeating the note's 'no mass-casualty or civilization-scale event' verbatim in sense; the researcher-survey detail re-states 5 / 10 / 38–51 before adding means, the 2022 round, and the NLP metasurvey; Innovation-First's detail re-cites the $109.1B vs $9.3B figures already carried in its description. Trim the repeated clause where convenient.

Compact→expanded ladder is done right where it matters most: the EU AI Act stat (staged-dates note → article-level phase-in and Digital Omnibus deferrals) and SB 53 (reporting-trigger note → revenue/compute scope, whistleblower channels, effective date) are both models of the intended pattern, as is every question 'detail'.

verdicts.critic: Above-fold selection is sound and reads at parity with a strong published topic. The six tier-1 basics span the debate's load-bearing axes without redundancy: stakes (researcher extinction estimates), pace (5x/yr compute growth), the EU regime, the present-harms evidence base (Incident Database), the US preemption fight named in why_now (99-1 Senate vote), and the first US frontier-specific state law (SB 53). None of the six is marginal, and the two demoted to T2 (compute-threshold comparison, Bletchley) plus the two at T3 (Council of Europe ratifications, extinction statement) are genuinely second-order relative to them. The four tier-1 questions cover the four decisions a reader has to make: how real and how soon the catastrophic risk is, whether the hazard is capability or deployment, who holds rule-writing authority, and whether binding rules cost a geopolitical lead. That last one carries the two highest-prevalence camps (Innovation-First at 80, National Security Realist), so it earns its slot. Positions cut at prevalence, and the six above the fold are the six highest-weighted, including every camp with weight 50 or above; the fold therefore shows the full architectural spread (deregulate, horizontal, frontier-only, sectoral, open-weights, security). No blocking defect on this dimension. Two boundary calls are debatable rather than wrong, and both are logged as notes: the EU-vs-California compute threshold sitting at T2 while a narrower SB 53 dollar figure sits at T1, and the present-harms axis being represented above the fold only by a stat, with both its question (T2) and its position (7th by prevalence) falling behind the fold.
notes: Basics T1/T2 boundary is defensible but the closest call in the set: the T2 'Training-compute threshold, in FLOP, that triggers binding duties · EU vs California' (10^26 vs 10^25) is the gate that decides who is regulated at all, and it is referenced by the T1 compute-growth note and by the T3 question on durable triggers. The T1 'Dollar threshold defining a reportable catastrophic AI incident · California SB 53' ($1 billion) is a definitional detail of one state's reporting duty. If a swap were ever wanted, that is the pair. Two reasons not to force it now: SB 53's label carries the first-US-frontier-law weight, and the threshold stat is wide:true, which would break the clean two-row 3-col grid that six narrow items currently produce.

No international item appears above the fold: all six T1 basics are US or EU domestic. Both international anchors (Bletchley, 28 countries incl. US and China, T2; Council of Europe ratifications, T3) sit behind 'Go deeper', even though 'who holds the pen: statehouse, capital, or treaty' is a T1 question and the crux's second axis. The tiering is still defensible because that T1 question and the crux subtitle both surface the axis above the fold, and Bletchley is a non-binding declaration rather than an operative regime. Worth watching if the international track hardens later.

The present-harms axis is thin above the fold on the opt-in layers: its question ('How should present, documented harms weigh against lower-probability catastrophic ones') is T2, and its position (Present-Harms Accountability, prevalence 45) sits 7th, just behind Open-Weights and National Security Realist at 50. This is coherent given scope_excluded explicitly removes hiring-bias audits, deepfakes, and job loss from the topic, and the T1 Incident Database stat plants the evidence anchor above the fold. But the ordering rests on a 50/50/45 near-tie, so the positions cut there is arbitrary rather than a genuine importance drop-off.

Positions are uniformly tier 1, so tier does no fold work in that section; the cut is entirely prevalence-driven. That is the documented render rule, and the top six are the right six, but it does mean the tier field carries no signal here and cannot be used to correct the 50/50/45 near-tie noted above.

Questions fold at 4/7 with a clean gradient: the four T1s are each a distinct decision, and the T3 ('Can regulators define enforceable, durable triggers') is correctly the deepest, since it presupposes answers to the ones above it. No reordering needed.

prevalence_basis.name: Innovation-First Competitor
prevalence_basis.sketch: Minimal binding rules and one light national standard; heavy regulation forfeits the AI race and the security that comes with winning it.

prevalence_basis.name: Comprehensive Regulator
prevalence_basis.sketch: Horizontal, risk-tiered law covering all AI, with the strictest binding duties on the most capable models, is the only durable public guarantee.

prevalence_basis.name: Frontier Safety Mandater
prevalence_basis.sketch: Target the handful of most capable models with mandatory testing, disclosure, whistleblower protection, and liability before deployment, not after harm.

prevalence_basis.name: Sectoral Incrementalist
prevalence_basis.sketch: Risk lives in uses, not models; let existing sector regulators extend proven rules to AI in medicine, finance, hiring, and beyond, case by case.

prevalence_basis.name: Global Coordinator
prevalence_basis.sketch: Frontier risk is transnational; only international agreements, shared evaluations, and compute governance can bind a worldwide race.

prevalence_basis.name: Pause Advocate
prevalence_basis.sketch: Smarter-than-human AI cannot be controlled with current science; halt frontier scaling until safety is demonstrated, by treaty if necessary.
